title: green arabia lake reveals 25000-year-old human life
dek: ancient lake shore held tools, animal bones and plant remains
body: At Uruq al-Julaybah in southern Saudi Arabia, researchers uncovered a 125,000-year-old lakeside where early humans left thousands of stone tools beside the bones of hippos and extinct buffalo. The site sits on what was once a freshwater lake, now buried beneath desert. Satellite terrain modelling reconstructed a lake 340 square kilometres across, fed by a greener climate during the Last Interglacial.

More than 500 plant and animal fossils were recovered from over 130 locations across the principal study area. Among the animal remains were hippopotamuses, long-horned buffaloes, camels, Arabian oryx, gazelles and ostriches. The presence of these species demonstrates how dramatically the environment differed from the arid landscape found in the region today.

The stone artefact assemblage numbers 5,511 items measuring more than two centimetres. Over 98 per cent were made from flint, and analysis shows prehistoric toolmakers used Levallois techniques to shape the stone. Microscopic and chemical examination of the tools has provided further evidence about how they were used.

Residues on the tools include traces of plants, some potentially toxic, and resin and woody tissue. These suggest that some stone implements were hafted onto wooden shafts and may have served as weapon tips. The presence of toxic plant compounds could represent some of the earliest evidence in Saudi Arabia for their possible use in hunting technology.

Other residues indicate that inhabitants processed tubers, shrubs and palm leaves, suggesting plants were exploited for food and a variety of practical activities. Evidence of palm-related vegetation is among the earliest identified in the region. The shores of Lake Mundafan appear to have supported stone tool production, the preparation of hunting equipment, animal and plant processing and the working of plant fibres.

"It is very exciting to see how the collaboration of so many different specialists allows us to reconstruct this uniquely complete picture of life, behaviour and the environment in the distant past," said Professor Frans van Buchem, KAUST Professor of Geology and co-lead scientist. "This site gives us a rare and richly detailed view of how people lived in a landscape that looks nothing like Arabia today," Professor Chris Clarkson, co-lead scientist and Professor of Archaeology at Griffith University, added.

The combination of stone tools, animal fossils and plant remains within the same securely dated archaeological context makes Uruq al-Julaybah particularly significant. Rather than providing isolated traces of prehistoric activity, the site allows researchers to reconstruct different aspects of daily life within the same landscape.
